vignette: ### Clinical Vignette for Alex Alex, a 21-year-old European male, has been struggling with post-traumatic stress symptoms following a traumatic event involving his younger sister. He was married and recently unemployed. The trauma began when he witnessed an assault on his sister at home, which left her severely injured but ultimately stable after hospitalization. Since the incident, Alex has been hyper-vigilant to perceived threats. People acting suspiciously, comments about his family, and specific body parts associated with the event are powerful triggers for him. These triggers frequently lead to intense flashbacks where he feels as if the assault is happening again. The smell of antiseptic from the hospital where she was treated often returns in these moments, adding a vivid sensory dimension to his recollections. Alex’s negative appraisals have intensified over time, leading to deep-seated feelings that his body is always on high alert despite being safe and that he is no longer capable of functioning as he once did. This has made him anxious about relying on himself, particularly in situations where he feels vulnerable or alone. These triggers often drive Alex into maladaptive strategies such as avoiding media with content similar to the assault, staying away from any situation where he might be alone, and even resorting to self-harm when overwhelmed by these emotions. His avoidance of TV programmes or films that remind him of the event is a direct response to his heightened threat monitoring, which puts him on guard at every sudden movement others make. The flashbacks are often so vivid that Alex says it’s like looking at photographs of the traumatic event in his mind. He struggles to put these experiences into words, leading to further emotional distress and reinforcing his belief that he can’t rely on himself to process or cope with them effectively. This self-doubt makes him even more sensitive to triggers. Over time, Alex has developed a vicious cycle where threats trigger flashbacks, which in turn lead him to maladaptive coping mechanisms like avoiding certain situations and places. He also engages in self-harm as an immediate but ineffective way to manage overwhelming feelings. These actions further exacerbate his negative appraisals about himself and his body's reactions. Alex’s marriage has been affected by these behaviors; he often avoids social gatherings or any situation where there might be triggers, leading to tension with his spouse. His unemployment also stems from his inability to focus on work when the memories of the event intrude so powerfully during the day. What finally brought Alex to seek help was a recent incident at home where he lashed out physically after mistaking a sudden movement for a threat related to his sister’s assault. This outburst deeply distressed him and made him realize that without intervention, his condition would continue to worsen, potentially affecting those closest to him. Alex is now looking for ways to regain control over his life and find more effective coping mechanisms. He hopes to reduce the intensity of his flashbacks and the frequency of his maladaptive behaviors so he can reconnect with his family and return to work. His current state leaves him afraid that his reactions will continue to harm those around him, but he is eager for a way out of this cycle. The traumatic event has left Alex feeling profoundly vulnerable and unable to trust his own reactions or abilities, making every small movement by others a potential trigger. This heightened threat monitoring leads directly into the maladaptive strategies he uses to cope with these overwhelming feelings, which in turn reinforces his negative appraisals about himself and his environment.
